We investigate the stellar mass-to-halo mass relation specifically targeting the evidence for its potential morphology-dependent variation. Direct optimization methods for control represent a distinct category within numerical optimal control theory. This study presents Complete Least Squares (CLS) as an framework for estimating the optimal location of moving objects from noisy observations. The method jointly estimates the trajectories of moving objects and their speeds by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between a smooth trajectory model (based on constant velocity) and the observation data. A primary advantage of CLS is that, unlike many filtering techniques requiring a known initial state, CLS functions as a smoother that integrates all available data from time $0$ to $T$ and does not depend on specific initial conditions or state probability densities at the starting point. Furthermore, the application of the CLS within a recursive structure enables efficient, real-time processing of observations as they arise. A theoretical examination of both minimum complete least squares and its adaptive recursive counterpart demonstrates asymptotic normality for joint speed and position estimators. This result establishes a formal basis for defining application-specific performance metrics, such as root mean square error (RMSE) and correlation. A computational simulation validates the accuracy and consistency of the CLS before detailing an implementation applied to infrared (IR) and high-speed camera data capturing targets in motion across multiple frames.

**We introduce a new tuning scheme for cameras called deep tinting, which uses deep neural networks to correct color inconsistencies between different lenses. Our tuning method is highly effective because a single trained network can address color errors between any pair of cameras, even if they were not seen during training. We tested this approach extensively on eight distinct cameras using combinations totaling 210 systems. To validate its efficacy, we released a dataset containing images from these varied cameras of nearly 1,200 different 3D objects (the "Multi-Tint" dataset), balanced and organized into eight equal groups for proper evaluation. We compare our technique against two existing approaches: traditional desaturation and white balance algorithms, as well as existing unsupervised methods. Our results show that it outperforms these existing techniques and establishes deep tinting as a valuable complement to other computer vision and rendering approaches.**

Our findings reveal that approximately half of all developers modify identical files simultaneously, representing significant frequency. Because this activity exhibits consistent patterns, we argue that techniques involving program analysis and machine learning—collectively known as meta-maintenance—can effectively propagate changes to such duplicate files with a high degree of success, making them suitable targets for general maintenance tasks.

Developing robust scalar field theory soliton frameworks is notoriously difficult, particularly for soliton networks. Nevertheless, several recent studies demonstrate that dropping $SO(2)$ invariance facilitates building effective theories for diverse applications, notably the critical phenomena of three-dimensional Ising models and lochite fields. In this work, we demonstrate the existence of solitons—specifically domain walls and vortices—within a class of $SO(2)$-broke theories. Our methodology leverages the successful strategy pioneered in literature for the $SO(2)$-invariant case. We modify our potential such that its minimum forms a one-dimensional interval; we subsequently identify soliton solutions by enforcing that the order parameter minimum aligns with this interval. Finally, we present initial indicators regarding the stability of these structures, revealing distinct differences between walls of non-degenerate scalar theories and those of degenerate theories due to extended solutions.

In real-world scenarios, agents frequently encounter environments characterized by partial observability and dynamic transition rules that are often beyond their control. Existing research in inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and inverse control (IRL/C) predominantly assumes static control models, limiting its applicability to contexts where environment dynamics fluctuate over time. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Hierarchical Probabilistic Dynamical Programming (HPDP), a methodology for inferring time-varying reward functions and time-invariant dynamical models from trajectories of both partially observability and control. By employing a hierarchical Bayesian framework, our approach learns a single shared model from diverse datasets, thereby enhancing data efficiency and interpretability. Experiments on HDPDP applied to a variety of benchmark problems indicate that it successfully recovers the true underlying environment dynamics reward structure more accurately than current state-of-the-art methods when trained on a mixture of heterogeneous trajectories. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that HDPDP exhibits significantly improved sample efficiency by leveraging shared patterns across multiple environments.

As modern mobile traffic continues to surge, there is an urgent need for enhanced data rates and service availability, driving research into future communication architectures that support multi-user, concurrent transmissions. This active area of study encompasses various power control approaches, including orthogonal methods, non-coherent schemes, and coherent techniques, each with distinct advantages and trade-offs. Given the diversity in these systems, comprehensively understanding the benefits and challenges of power control across different frameworks is essential for effectively deploying emerging power-control-based architectures in next-generation power management strategies. Consequently, this paper provides a detailed review and analysis of current power control approaches for multi-user wireless systems designed around concurrent transmission, offering an informative perspective to guide future developments in this cutting-edge field.

The system also significantly diminishes risks associated with data privacy leaks and substantially lowers costs for storing and transmitting sensitive datasets.

Kernelization serves as a central element in contemporary NLP systems, streamlining text representation to improve computational efficiency and model generalization. Despite these advantages, kernelization is inherently vulnerable to text manipulation attacks. An effective attack seeks to incur the minimal possible performance degradation on a target text classification task while simultaneously maximizing the increase observed in a victim text classification target. To address this, the study reformulates attack and defense strategies as a zero-sum game between an attacker optimizing for performance gain and the system's integrity versus the attacker. First, the text manipulation problem is formalized within the kernelization framework of text classification. Next, an optimal, albeit possibly unequation, attack is constructed using Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP). Subsequently, an optimal counter-measure is defined through a Min-Max formulation of Linear Programming (LP). Finally, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of proposed attacks and defenses when applied to key text classification tasks, including financial sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and hate speech detection.

Global aggregation techniques are essential for enabling privacy-preserving analysis and machine learning in federated environments and distributed systems. This study reexamines research on optimal transport (OT)-based aggregation, a field currently in its formative stages, by addressing three pivotal inquiries. First is feasibility: Is OT-based aggregation possible? While the answer appears affirmative—since any pair of distributions from a fixed family can be optimally transported—this seems trivial. The real challenge lies scalability: Can we design an efficient "per-local" OT that avoids full re-transport when clients' data distributions change? Existing solutions include quantization and "earthmover distance" (EMD) truncations, which sacrifice certain privacy guarantees in exchange for local computability. Alternatively, we can leverage the duality between OT and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to frame the problem as finding a "local EMD minimizer." This transforms a non-smoothly differentiable local objective of dimension $2n_k$ into a smooth one reduced to $n_k$ dimensions. Additionally, to address variance, we introduce a "multi-step stochastic EMD" algorithm. Finally, these methodologies were validated on synthetic datasets and the practical scenario of consistent auto-encoding, revealing significant computational gains over current state-of-the-art OT aggregators depending on the chosen data dimension $n_k$.

External links play a critical role in Community-Maintained Sites like Stack Overflow, facilitating the exchange of extensive code repositories, documentation, and point-of-view analyses. Ultimately, we discuss these findings in relation to future research and offer strategic recommendations to both users and administrators.

Non-i.i.d. data distributions constitute a fundamental challenge in federated learning (FL), often obstructing successful convergence and compelling clients to employ advanced techniques like tunable curvature and robust initialization to compensate for severe bias in local updates. We introduce the Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation (BAA) algorithm, executed locally on client devices without requiring any special modifications to standard stochastic gradient descent. BAA operates according to gradient buffers that merge gradients from multiple local steps; once filled, this buffer transmits the accumulated gradients to the server. Our analysis reveals that this lightweight approach significantly cuts communication loads by a factor proportional to the number of gradients within the buffer. Furthermore, we establish a specific bias regarding these non-i.i.d. partitions, then derive corresponding bounds on this bias as functions of the buffer size, number of clients, gradients, variance, and bias. Our findings demonstrate that for square loss problems, the bias produced by BAA matches that which would occur with ideal, infinite-size communication batches. The experimental outcomes regarding standard federated stochastic gradient descent confirm that BAA achieves performance nearly indistinguishable from both vanilla FL and algorithms that explicitly correct for bias in their optimization processes, all while reducing communication costs by orders of magnitude.

Detecting multiband microwave and terahertz radiation emitted during quantum dot transitions has long been hindered by the inherent low signal strength. Although dedicated amplification and rapid sampling were previously thought essential to overcome this challenge, our research demonstrates an alternative: a rapidly functioning digital detector capable of capturing weak Rydberg emissions without prior amplification. By leveraging digital deconvolution and trained on simulated datasets, a deep learning-based Autocorrelation Network successfully recovered the original waveform from artificial data with nearly perfect fidelity. When applied to real experimental contexts, this autonomous method reduced weak microwave tera-hertz (Rydberg) signals rising by an order of magnitude of approximately 40 dB. Notably, it achieves these results while maintaining precise temporal localization without needing a faster sample rate or upfront amplification. Consequently, this methodology equips researchers with flexible Rydberg detection techniques, allowing the existing weak-signal detection and control mechanisms to remain both robust and cost-effective.

This study examines a visually directed form of sound synthesis—visually directed sound synthesis (VDS)—which involves a generative component, specifically Graph-Based Sound Synthesis (GBSS). In VDS-GBSS, a sound engineer first creates an audio graph featuring synths and effect processors linked by specific relationships. These connections inform a neural network trained on both the audio and the audio graph. Once the complete neural network learns both the audio and the audio graph well enough, sound engineers can modify the audio graph by adding, removing, or replacing nodes and their connecting relationships. These modifications should result in corresponding alterations to the sound that can be clearly understood. Although initial attempts exist, current research struggles to provide an intuitive method for modifying audio graphs; therefore, this research explores using those modifications in the domain of 3-D visualizations. In this approach, sound engineers change 3-D visualizations instead of audio graphs, with each modification mapped to a specific alteration in audio through another neural network that can "learn" how modifications in three-D visualizations affect audio. The results show this research provides an intuitive modification method for audio graph that supports VDS-GBSS, improving current techniques.

In many real-world scenarios, data exists as time-series collections of objects where individual elements contain sub-sequences, meaning the entire dataset represents temporal information. Additionally, objects may belong to specific states or classes, creating dependent states across the group that vary based on their own time evolution. Consequently, capturing temporal links between objects and their state conditions is vital for effective modeling. Previous research has addressed acquiring temporal dependence for univariate objects, yet acquiring temporal dependence between objects within dependent states remains largely unexploited. Additionally, while extracting temporal interactions across consecutive time steps for data sets is currently unresolved, this approach is necessary. This study proposes addressing these issues by constructing data sets through latent state estimation via Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to represent both the global state of the object group and its individual components. By applying recurrent neural networks, we learn features exhibiting dependencies at adjacent time steps while considering both the overall and individual temporal patterns. This paper explores how Galileo's background in mathematics influenced his revolutionary contributions to physics and philosophy, highlighting his belief in the primacy of mathematical proof over sensory experience.
